## A nineteenth-century surprise {#gac1-weierstrass-history .gac-lesson }

<ul class="gac-history-bullets">
<li>Many nineteenth-century mathematicians expected continuous functions to be differentiable apart from <strong>exceptional points</strong>.</li>
<li>An isolated corner seemed to fit that picture: a graph could remain continuous even when its derivative failed to exist at a particular point.</li>
<li>In <strong>1872</strong>, Weierstrass presented a counterexample: a function that was <strong>continuous everywhere, but differentiable nowhere</strong>.</li>
</ul>

::: notes
Allow about 1 minute, then show the function on the next slide. Emphasise that this challenged a widespread expectation, not a theorem or a belief held by every nineteenth-century mathematician. An isolated corner was familiar; failure of differentiability at every point was much more surprising.

Weierstrass presented his famous construction to the Berlin Academy on 18 July 1872. The proof was published by Paul du Bois-Reymond in 1875. Earlier examples existed, including Bolzano's unpublished construction, so avoid claiming that Weierstrass was the first to discover the possibility. The definitions of continuity and differentiability already existed; the counterexample reinforced the importance of distinguishing them.

Transition: “How can we build such a function? We add waves that become smaller in height, but oscillate more rapidly.”

Sources: Allan Pinkus, Weierstrass and Approximation Theory, pp. 3–5, https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/hat/fpapers/wap.pdf ; MacTutor, The function concept, https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Functions/ .
:::
